articles.title: Promoting equity, diversity and inclusion in intensive Care: a position paper of the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine.
Scientific Output in Septic Shock According to Country Income and Gender: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
articles.abstract: We aimed to assess trends in septic shock publications by country income and author gender. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for articles indexed with "septic shock" between January 2014 and December 2024. All peer-reviewed publication types were eligible. Conference abstracts and non-peer-reviewed material were excluded. Bibliographic data, first and last author affiliations, country income level (World Bank classification: low- and middle-income countries [LMICs] and high-income countries [HICs]), and journal prestige (SCImago Journal Rank [SJR]) were extracted. Author gender was inferred using the NamSor application programming interface (API). Of 10,352 eligible publications, LMIC-affiliated first authors increased over time (+2.13% per year; 95% CI, +1.66 to +2.61; p < 0.001) from 18% in 2014 to 37% in 2024. Women represented 35.6% of first authors and 25.0% of last authors (with around 20% of authors not classifiable by the NamSor API), with higher proportions in LMICs than HICs (p < 0.001) for both first authors (44.5% vs. 32.5%) and last authors (35.2% vs. 21.5%). Gender concordance was more frequent, with female first authors more often paired with female last authors than male first authors (31.7% vs. 21.1%). Cross-income collaborations, especially involving LMIC last authors, remained rare. Articles led by men in HICs were more often published in higher-SJR journals compared with those led by women (p < 0.001), whereas no gender differences were observed among LMIC-affiliated authors. Despite encouraging growth in LMIC contributions and female representation, major inequities persist. Strengthening equitable collaborations and supporting underrepresented groups would broaden participation and enhance the global applicability in critical care research.

articles.title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
articles.abstract: Cluster-randomized clinical trials (cRCTs) are pooled with individually randomized clinical trials (iRCTs) in meta-analyses. However, cRCTs are associated with methodological characteristics potentially inducing systematic differences compared with iRCTs. In acute settings, trial inclusion is time-sensitive, exacerbating inclusion-based biases. We conducted a meta-epidemiological study to assess deviations in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs in these settings. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase. We screened and identified all meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, or critical care within the last decade that included at least one cRCT and one iRCT. Data were extracted in duplicate from the meta-analyses. If overlapping trials were identified, results were pooled. The primary outcome was mortality; the secondary outcome comprised length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes. Using absolute ln(odds ratio [OR]) for mortality and absolute Hedges' g for the secondary outcome, mean differences (MDs) in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs were analyzed using mixed regression models, presented with 95% CIs. We identified 94 eligible meta-analyses; 44.7% reported on randomization type (cRCT or iRCT). We included 65 meta-analyses in quantitative analyses, encompassing 212 randomized clinical trials (39 cRCTs and 173 iRCTs) and 315,276 patients. No statistically significant difference in absolute ln(OR) for mortality between cRCTs and iRCTs was found (MD, -0.110; 95% CI, -0.093 to 0.313). For length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, a significant difference in absolute Hedges' g was found (MD, -0.202; 95% CI, -0.392 to -0.012). A systematic difference between cRCTs and iRCTs in length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, but not mortality, was identified, with cRCTs reporting smaller effect size magnitudes than iRCTs. With under half of identified meta-analyses reporting on randomization modality, these results highlight the need for improved transparency and statistical consideration of randomization type in future meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, and critical care.

articles.title: Furosemide Stress Test in Adults and Children With Acute Kidney Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic utility of the furosemide stress test (FST) for acute kidney injury (AKI) management in critically ill adults and children. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception to March 3, 2026. Studies evaluating the standardized FST protocol in critically ill adults or children with AKI were eligible. Outcomes included AKI stage 3 progression (Q1), kidney replacement therapy (KRT) initiation (Q2), short-term mortality (Q3), successful KRT liberation (Q4), and FST-guided vs. standard KRT initiation in randomized trials (Q5). Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 and Risk of Bias 2. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Twenty studies (n = 1979; 11 countries; 2013-2025) were included. For AKI progression (nine studies; n = 501), pooled sensitivity was 0.69 and specificity was 0.88 (area under the curve [AUC], 0.89; GRADE: low). For KRT initiation (nine studies; n = 952), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.75 (AUC, 0.79; GRADE: very low). For mortality (six studies; n = 487), sensitivity was 0.56 and specificity was 0.76 (AUC, 0.75; GRADE: very low). For KRT liberation (three studies; n = 177), sensitivity was 0.81 and specificity was 0.87 (AUC, 0.89; GRADE: low for sensitivity, very low for specificity). The effect of FST-guided early KRT initiation on short-term mortality was uncertain (pooled risk ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.79-1.27; two randomized controlled trials, n = 212; GRADE: very low). Pediatric analyses yielded AUC values of 0.81 and 0.63 for KRT initiation and mortality, respectively. Based on low to very low certainty evidence, the FST may support risk stratification for AKI progression and KRT liberation in critically ill adults. Its impact on mortality when guiding early KRT initiation remains uncertain. As a low-cost bedside test, the FST can be a useful tool in resource-limited settings where novel biomarkers are inaccessible.

Delay From Hypotension Onset to Appropriate Antifungal Therapy Initiation Is the Critical Determinant of Outcome in Candida Septic Shock.
authors: and the Cooperative Antimicrobial Therapy of Septic Shock (CATSS) Database Research Group
articles.abstract: To determine the effect of delays in initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy from the initial onset of persistent hypotension to the outcome of Candida septic shock. Retrospective cohort study. A total of 32 academic and community hospitals in Canada, the United States, and Saudi Arabia (July 1989 to June 2018). A total of 850 adult patients with culture-positive Candida septic shock. None. Out of 850 patients with Candida septic shock, 69.2% patients (589) received appropriate antifungal therapy after the onset of persistent hypotension. A strong relationship was observed between the delay in initiation of pathogen-appropriate antifungal (PAA) therapy and hospital survival. The adjusted odds ratio of death was 1.045 per hour of delay (95% CI, 1.035-1.056; p < 0.0001). The survival rate was 86% when an appropriate antifungal for the isolated pathogen was administered within 2 hours of the initial documentation of persistent hypotension. Thereafter, hospital survival decreased an average of 5.0% per hour for each hour of delay to 10-12 hours of delay. In a multivariate analysis, which included the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score and epidemiologic/therapeutic variables, the time to initiation of appropriate antifungal therapy emerged as the single strongest predictor of outcome. Sensitivity analysis further demonstrated that the adverse effects of delayed antifungal treatment were consistent across various subgroups, including different types of infections, pathogens, and antifungal drug classes. Median time to appropriate antifungal therapy was 32.3 hours (interquartile range, 11.2-66.0 hr), with only 16.9% receiving therapy within 6 hours of hypotension onset. Administration of PAAs within the first hours of documented hypotension significantly improved hospital survival. Less than 20% of patients received appropriate antifungals within 6 hours of documented hypotension.

articles.title: Rethinking Oliguria in the ICU: From Threshold to Trajectory.
Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

Dyspnea during resting breathing and carbon dioxide rebreathing in adult patients with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome.
articles.abstract: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is an ultra-rare genetic disorder caused by PHOX2B mutations. Patients lack central CO2 chemosensitivity and require ventilatory support during sleep. Children with CCHS have been reported to lack CO2-induced air hunger, but respiratory sensations and dyspnea have not been characterized in adults. Do genetically characterized adult CCHS patients experience respiratory sensations and dyspnea during unassisted resting breathing and CO2 rebreathing, and along which dimensions? This was a prospective controlled observational study conducted on a convenience sample derived from a national cohort of an ultrarare disease. Thirteen adult CCHS patients carrying PHOX2B mutations underwent Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile (MDP) assessment during unassisted resting breathing and at the end of CO2 rebreathing. Healthy controls were studied under the same conditions. Before the study, none of the patients had spontaneously reported dyspnea or bothersome respiratory sensations. When prompted with the MDP during resting breathing, 9/13 patients described breathing unpleasantness (non-zero MDP-A1) versus 0/18 controls (p < 0.0001), and 12/13 fulfilled criteria for dyspnea defined as breathing awareness associated with negative affect. During CO2 rebreathing, ventilatory responses remained profoundly blunted, yet breathing unpleasantness increased. Compared with controls, patients had lower sensory and affective ratings, with less frequent air hunger (p = 0.0108). MDP ratings did not correlate with ventilatory response to CO2 or genotype. Adult CCHS patients can experience conscious unpleasant breathing awareness at rest and retain a perceptual response to CO2 despite abolished or nearly abolished central chemosensitivity. These findings suggest respiratory interoceptive pathways beyond canonical brainstem chemosensitive circuits and support active multidimensional assessment of dyspnea in adult CCHS patients.

articles.title: Fatigue, Anxiety and Depression 12 Months After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Population Based Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: To determine the prevalence and factors associated with fatigue, anxiety, and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); examine their associations with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and functional recovery; and compare symptom burden with population norms. This prospective, population-based cohort study included adults (≥18 years) who received EMS-attempted resuscitation and survived to hospital discharge following non-traumatic OHCA in Victoria, Australia, between July 2019 and June 2022. Survivors were identified from a statewide OHCA registry and completed a 12-month telephone interview. Primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Secondary outcomes included HRQoL (EQ-5D, SF-12), functional recovery (GOSE), living arrangement, and return to work. Of 1068 eligible 12-month survivors, 728 (68.2%) completed follow-up (median age 61 years; 555 [76.2%] male). Fatigue was reported by 35.8% (250/699), anxiety by 22.6% (162/716), and depression by 18.0% (129/716). Higher symptom burden was associated with lower EQ-5D and SF-12 scores, worse GOSE outcomes (all p<0.001) and reduced return-to-work rates. Compared with population norms, survivors reported greater fatigue (SMD 0.64; 95%CI, 0.50-0.78;p<0.001), and depression (SMD, 0.12; 95%CI, 0.02,0.21;p=0.02) but lower anxiety (SMD, -0.27; 95%CI, -0.35 to -0.18;p<0.001). In adjusted models, younger age, preexisting anxiety or depression, diabetes and initial non-shockable arrest were associated with higher symptom burden, whereas EMS-witnessed arrests were associated with lower symptom burden. Fatigue, anxiety, and depression were common at 12 months after OHCA and are associated with poorer recovery. Fatigue exceeded population norms and may be an under-recognised component of cardiac arrest survivorship.

articles.title: Regional implementation of a prehospital advanced life support program with video-assisted physician direction and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: The smart advanced life support (SALS) program was introduced to provide prehospital advanced life support under real-time video-assisted physician direction for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This study evaluated the association between regional SALS implementation and OHCA outcomes. This retrospective cohort study used difference-in-differences and event-study analyses with data from the OHCA surveillance system in South Korea and included adult OHCA cases (aged ≥19 years) from 2 years before through 4 years after SALS implementation in August 2015. The exposure was region-level implementation of SALS. Outcomes were the prehospital time interval, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to discharge, and favorable neurological outcome. Pre- to post-implementation changes were compared between regions with and without SALS. A total of 129,207 cases were included. SALS regions had greater increases in the prehospital time interval (4.12 minutes; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.91 to 5.33) and prehospital ROSC (1.35 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.56 to 2.15) than regions without SALS. No significant additional improvements were observed in survival to discharge (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.31 to 0.62) or favorable neurological outcome (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.08 to 0.37). Event-study analyses suggested differential pre-intervention trends for prehospital time, but not for the other outcomes. SALS regions showed greater increases in prehospital time and prehospital ROSC without significant improvements in survival to discharge or favorable neurological outcome, but the finding for prehospital time should be interpreted cautiously because differential pre-intervention trends were observed.

articles.title: Association Between Capnographic Changes During Pulse Checks of Varying Durations and Clinical Outcomes During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Multicenter Study From Türkiye (CaPTuRe).
articles.abstract: To investigate the association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of different durations and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) outcomes. This multicenter, prospective, controlled, quasi-randomized study categorized patients according to pulse check duration: Group A (≤5 seconds) and Group B (>5 to ≤10 seconds). Five measurements were obtained during the first six CPR cycles. Four capnographic parameters were evaluated for each measurement: Post-CPR end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2), Pre-CPR ETCO2, loss rate (percentage decrease between Post- and Pre-CPR ETCO2), and recovery time (time required to regain the previous cycle's Post-CPR ETCO2). The study included 252 cardiac arrest patients (Group A, n=124; Group B, n=128). In Group A, patients with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) had markedly lower loss rates and shorter recovery times than non-survivors, together with higher pre- and post-CPR ETCO2 values (all p<0.001). Group A also had a higher ROSC rate than Group B (36.3% vs. 19.5%; p=0.005). Logistic regression identified pulse check duration as an independent predictor of ROSC, with Group A having 2.39-fold higher odds of ROSC than Group B (odds ratio [OR]=2.39, 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.347-4.242; p=0.003). Pre-CPR ETCO2 was strongly negatively correlated with loss rate (ρ=-0.770), whereas Pre- and Post-CPR ETCO2 values (ρ=0.96) and loss rate and recovery time (ρ=0.89) were strongly positively correlated. Pulse checks completed within 5 seconds were associated with more favorable capnographic dynamics and higher ROSC rates than those lasting 6-10 seconds. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective validation.

articles.title: Identifying the Operational Bottleneck to Shock Delivery After Automated External Defibrillator Activation.
articles.abstract: Cardiac arrest registries record automated external defibrillator (AED) use and shock delivery but not post-activation operational timing. We aimed to identify the largest measurable bottleneck and an exploratory pad-application target for shock delivery within 60 seconds of AED power-on. We retrospectively analyzed timestamps from remotely monitored Nihon Kohden AEDs between January 2018 and February 2026. After excluding inspection records, we grouped records into activation events and quantified intervals. Shock-timing and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were restricted to initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery. We analyzed 8,115 activation events. Median times were 42 seconds (interquartile range [IQR], 30-56) from power-on to completion of pad application, nine seconds (IQR, 9-11) from pad application to the first analysis, and 52 seconds (IQR, 40-66) from power-on to the first analysis endpoint. The power-on-to-pad-application interval accounted for a median of 81% (IQR, 75-85) of the total power-on-to-first-analysis interval, increasing to 87% (IQR, 85-90) when first analysis occurred more than 60 seconds after power-on. Among 900 initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery, the median pad-application-to-shock interval was 15 seconds (IQR 13-17). Exploratory ROC analysis yielded a power-on to pad-application threshold of ≥ 51 seconds in relation to first recorded shock delivery occurring more than 60 seconds after AED power-on. The interval from AED power-on to electronically detected completion of pad application, encompassing all intervening actions, was the largest measurable post-activation bottleneck. Completion within 50 seconds may serve as an exploratory process target for first recorded shock delivery within 60 seconds among initially shock-advised events.

articles.title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.
authors: Pittsburgh Post Cardiac Arrest Service Investigators
articles.abstract: Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), normal jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO2 gap, and lower intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns. This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO2 or PbtO2 monitoring. We categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and SjvO2, PbCO2 gap, PbtO2, and ICP. The SjvO2 and PbtO2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. SjvO2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β=3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), butwas higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β=12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO2 gap compared to malignant (β=-1.4; 95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β=-2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. PbtO2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant patterns in our adjusted model (β=4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β=-19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). Interpretation BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.

articles.title: Real-time feedback during bag-valve-mask ventilation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a before-and-after study (VEntilation during Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation Study, VECARS-2).
authors: Paris Fire Brigade Cardiac Arrest Task Force (collaborators)
articles.abstract: This study compared bag-valve-mask ventilation quality and adherence to the guideline-recommended ventilation volume range during 30:2 cardiopulmonary resuscitation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest before and after the implementation of real-time feedback. We conducted a before-and-after observational study of two sequential adult cohorts with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest managed by basic life support teams from the Paris Fire Brigade. A bidirectional sensor measured insufflated volume (Vi) and expiratory tidal volume (Vt). The display was masked during Period-1 and provided real-time feedback during Period-2. We assessed adherence to the guideline-recommended range using mixed-effects regression; we analyzed Vt and leak volume using gamma log-link generalized linear mixed models. We analyzed 4,300 ventilations in 163 patients, 96 without feedback and 67 with feedback. Median Vi was lower with feedback (471 mL) than without (513 mL, p=0.03 for the first ventilation of each cycle) but median Vt was unchanged (235 vs. 243 mL, p=0.84). Vi dispersion was reduced by 35% (mean within-patient IQR ratio 0.65 [95%-CI, 0.53-0.77]). Vi was 400-600 mL in 68% of ventilations with feedback vs. 42% without feedback. In contrast, Vt was 400-600 mL in only 14% of ventilations with feedback vs. 15% without feedback. In multivariable analysis, leak volume was 12% lower with feedback (mean ratio, 0.88 [95%-CI, 0.77-0.99]). Real-time feedback was associated with improved adherence to the guideline-recommended range for Vi, less dispersed Vi,and lower leak volume. Causal inference, clinical significance, and generalizability warrant further evaluation.

articles.title: Assessment of Tidal Volume in Patients Undergoing Noninvasive Ventilation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is widely used in acute respiratory failure (ARF), yet the association between high tidal volume (Vt) and clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined. We evaluated the association between Vt and NIV failure overall and by ARF type, and its relationship with respiratory and clinical outcomes. MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and Latin American and Caribbean Health Science Literature (1976 to September 2025). Observational studies of adults with ARF treated with NIV reporting Vt or Vt normalized to predicted body weight (Vt/PBW) in NIV success and failure groups. Three pairs of reviewers identified studies and extracted data independently. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Risk of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. Eleven studies (1136 patients) were included. Vt/PBW was higher in NIV failure vs. success (mean difference [MD], 1.02 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.60-1.45 mL/kg]), whereas absolute Vt did not differ (MD, 1.30 [-33.31 to 35.91]). In hypoxemic ARF, Vt/PBW remained higher in NIV failure (MD, 0.89 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.04-1.73 mL/kg]); no data were available for hypercapnic ARF. Post hoc analyses showed that higher Vt/PBW was associated with increased mortality (odds ratio, 9.11; 95% CI, 3.88-21.37), higher respiratory rate (RR; MD, 3.14 breaths/min [95% CI, 1.36-4.92 breaths/min]), and lower Paco2 (MD, -2.38 mm Hg [95% CI, -4.16 to -0.5938 mm Hg]), but no with pressure support (PS) level (MD, 0.24 [95% CI, -0.81 to 1.29]). Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. In adults with ARF treated with NIV, higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure and worse outcomes. These findings reflect prognostic associations rather than causality, and interventional studies with systematic Vt monitoring are needed. Importantly, elevated Vt/PBW, higher RR, lower Paco2, and increased mortality, without differences in PS, collectively implicate elevated respiratory drive as a driver of increased mortality (PROSPERO [CRD42024584977]).Findings: Higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure, particularly in hypoxemic respiratory failure; post hoc analyses showed associations with increased mortality, higher respiratory rate, and lower Paco2.

Fertility, pregnancy, and women's health in bronchiectasis: a multicenter study and ELF-EMBARC patient survey.
articles.abstract: Bronchiectasis in women of reproductive age is increasingly recognized, yet data on fertility and pregnancy outcomes remain limited. What are fertility characteristics, pregnancy outcomes, and patient-reported reproductive health experiences in women with bronchiectasis? We conducted a multicenter, retrospective cohort study across EMBARC-affiliated centers including women with bronchiectasis and pregnancy between 2012 and 2023. Clinical, pulmonary, obstetric, and neonatal data were collected. In parallel, an international patient survey assessed fertility, pregnancy, and hormonal influences on disease. Statistical analyses included comparative and correlation testing. Eighty-three women contributed data from 121 pregnancies and 123 neonates. Mean age at conception was 29.5 years. Assisted reproductive technologies were used in 32.1% of pregnancies, more frequently in primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) than other etiologies (48.5% vs. 8.7%, P=0.004). Lung function remained stable during and after pregnancy. Exacerbations occurred in 58.6% of pregnancies. Mean gestational age was 38 weeks and mean birth weight was 2.99 kg. Pre-pregnancy FEV1 correlated with birth weight (ρ=0.42, P=0.001) and gestational age (ρ=0.25, P=0.042). Neonatal outcomes were generally favorable. Survey data (n=629) demonstrated an early onset of menopause in women with bronchiectasis diagnosed before age 50 years compared to after 50 years. Women with PCD reported difficulties conceiving more often than women with early onset bronchiectasis without PCD. Pregnancy in women with bronchiectasis is frequently complicated by exacerbations and low neonatal birth weight. Subfertility is primarily driven by PCD, while non-PCD bronchiectasis shows rates similar to the general population. Pre-pregnancy lung function is associated with neonatal outcomes, supporting the importance of pulmonary optimization and multidisciplinary care before and during pregnancy.

articles.title: Striving for Equity in Cystic Fibrosis Research: Perspectives from Black and Hispanic/ Latino(a) Individuals with CF.
articles.abstract: Black and Hispanic people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF) experience worse health outcomes. Health disparities are exacerbated by clinical research that does not adequately represent the diversity of the CF population. How do Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino(a) PwCF perceive clinical research? What are the barriers and facilitators to participation in research? Are there viable solutions to improve inclusion? Semi-structured, individual interviews were conducted with PwCF aged ≥18 years who identify as Black/African American race and/or Hispanic/Latino(a) ethnicity. Participants were recruited from six geographically diverse CF centers and through CF Foundation Community Voice, a CF community partner organization. The interview guide was created by a committee that included minoritized PwCF, research coordinators, and physician-scientists. Thematic analysis with inductive and deductive coding was used to analyze interview transcripts. Twenty PwCF were interviewed from 2024 to 2025. Drawing from a race-conscious adaptation of the Behavioral Model for Vulnerable Populations, we used domains of predisposing, need-based, and healthcare environment factors, as well as emergent themes relating to information and support needs. Participants discussed barriers to research participation that included narrow eligibility criteria (e.g., genotype requirements, health status) and logistical challenges such as time and cost. PwCF described a sense of isolation as persons of color with CF, which impacted sense of trust in CF care and research studies. They highlighted that racialized experiences, especially doubt surrounding their CF diagnosis, significantly impact willingness to participate. Solutions center around providing community support to address feelings of isolation and information needs to provide transparency about study design and intent. Participation in clinical research is strongly influenced by an interplay of social, cultural, health, and systemic factors. Solutions to improve inclusion in trials center the needs of marginalized communities across all phases of study design and implementation.

articles.title: Weathering the storm: Predictors and resource burden of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity after severe traumatic brain injury.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Reported incidence of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) after severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) approaches one-third, largely from cohorts that excluded early deaths. Predictors and resource consequences remain unclear. We identified predictors of PSH development and associations between diagnosis, PSH Assessment Measure (PSH-AM) subscores [clinical features scale (CFS) and diagnosis likelihood tool (DLT)], and resource utilization. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with severe TBI admitted to a tertiary care center intensive care unit (ICU) (October 2020-September 2025), stratified by PSH diagnosis. Two reviewers assigned PSH-AM scores. PSH cannot be diagnosed until the syndrome declares itself over days, so exposure is conditioned on survival; mortality is reported descriptively. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of PSH diagnosis. Log-transformed linear regressions estimated associations of PSH diagnosis and subscores with hospital length of stay (LOS), ICU LOS, and ventilator days. Thirty-day composite outcomes, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and landmark analysis evaluated robustness. Of 509 patients with severe TBI, 86 (17%) developed PSH. Younger age [odds ratio (OR): 0.97 (95% CI: 0.96-0.98); P<0.001) and higher ISS [1.05 (1.02-1.07); P<0.001] independently predicted PSH. PSH was associated with longer hospital LOS (372.9%), ICU LOS (278.3%), and more ventilator days (266.4%; all P<0.001). Mortality was 11.6% (PSH) versus 35.9% (non-PSH). IPTW demonstrated PSH had fewer days alive and out of hospital (-46.8%; P<0.001) and landmark analysis highlighted fewer ventilator-free days (-40.2%; P=0.0097) and ICU-free days (-46.9%; P<0.001). Higher DLT subscores were associated with longer hospital (36.3%; P=0.001) and ICU (23.3%; P=0.005) stays, whereas the CFS subscore showed no associations. The PSH diagnosis is contingent on survival. Younger patients with severe TBI who survive their initial injuries are more likely to develop PSH and occupy hospital beds meaningfully longer. The diagnosis likelihood tool, not the clinical features scale, tracks with that burden. Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

articles.title: Wrong hospital, wrong outcome: Impact of care fragmentation following trauma laparotomy.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Care fragmentation (CF), defined as readmission to a nonindex hospital, has been identified as a potential predictor of poor outcomes after traumatic injury. Trauma laparotomy (TL) is a common procedure with perioperative risk of complications and readmission. Incidence of CF following TL, its risk factors, and its effects on outcomes are unknown. We hypothesized that CF after TL is associated with increased mortality during hospital readmission compared with continuity of care (CC). The Nationwide Readmissions Database (2016-2022) was queried for hospitalized adult (≥18) patients with traumatic injury and open surgery of gastrointestinal or genitourinary systems during index admission, and unplanned readmission within 90 days. Demographics, comorbidities, injury severity, procedures, and disposition data were collected for patients with CF and compared with patients with CC. The primary outcome was in-hospital death during readmission. Univariate comparisons and multivariable logistic regression were performed. A total of 14,773 TL patients were included in the analysis. From these, 2,059 (13.9%) were readmitted within 90 days. The average age of readmitted patients was 43 years, and the majority (68.6%) were male. Of the readmissions, 441 (21.4%) experienced CF. Discharge home from the index admission was associated with lower odds of CF (OR 0.52, 95% CI: 0.32-0.84, p=0.008). On multivariable regression analysis, CF was significantly associated with in-hospital death during readmission (OR 5.09, 95% CI: 1.22-21.16, p=0.03). CF is common following TL and is associated with an increased risk of death on readmission, even after adjustment for baseline comorbidities and other hospital characteristics. Patients who are discharged home are less likely to experience CF. TL survivors may represent a patient population that would benefit from targeted efforts to reduce CF. Therapeutic; Level III.

articles.title: Infections Acquired in the ICU Among Cancer and Other Immunosuppressed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: To compare the cumulative incidence of ICU-acquired infections (ICU-AIs) across distinct immunosuppression diagnostic categories (solid cancer, hematological cancer, other immunosuppression) and nonimmunosuppressed patients, accounting for competing risks of death and discharge. Retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data. A total of 50 participating ICUs in Brazil. A total of 38,126 adult patients admitted between October 2019 and December 2021 with an ICU stay exceeding 48 hours and no infections diagnosed within the first 48 hours. None. The primary outcome was the incidence of the first ICU-AI during the ICU stay, evaluated using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR). In the multivariable competing-risk analysis, patients with hematological malignancies (sHR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.01-2.65) and other immunosuppressive conditions (sHR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.02-2.54) were associated with an increased cumulative incidence of ICU-AI, while solid malignancy was not significantly different from non-immunosuppressed patients (sHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.68-1.14). Patients with hematological malignancies and other immunosuppressive conditions face a significantly higher risk of ICU-AIs.

articles.title: Irisin is associated with survival in sepsis and attenuates macrophage pro-inflammatory responses with involvement of AMPK signaling.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, yet effective targeted therapies remain limited. We evaluated the prognostic significance of irisin, a myokine, in sepsis cohort and examined its immunomodulatory effects on macrophages using a translational approach. Patients were enrolled in a prospectively collected sepsis registry and biobank. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was conducted to assess independent association between irisin and 30-day mortality. Mechanistic studies used macrophages ex vivo and a murine cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model. Higher serum irisin was independently associated with lower 30-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.955, 95% confidence interval 0.913-0.999, p=0.044) in patients with sepsis (N=655). Irisin showed modest discrimination for 30-day mortality (AUROC 0.609), with no statistically significant difference from lactate (AUROC 0.652; p=0.145). In vitro , irisin suppressed LPS-induced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, preserved AMPK phosphorylation, attenuated IκBα degradation, and reduced pro-inflammatory markers in macrophages. Several of these cellular effects were attenuated following AMPKα1 depletion. In vivo , irisin improved 7-day survival after CLP (75% vs. 36%, p<0.05) and reduced systemic inflammatory cytokines at 24 hours. Higher serum irisin was independently associated with lower 30-day mortality in patients with sepsis, although its standalone discriminatory performance was modest. Experimental findings further showed that irisin improved survival and attenuated macrophage inflammatory responses, with AMPK signaling contributing to several cellular effects. These findings support further evaluation of irisin as part of integrated prognostic assessment and investigation of irisin-related signaling in sepsis.

articles.title: Making blood work: Toward precision care after cardiac arrest.
Decision volume and temporal workload structure as dissociable correlates of fatigue and mood in intensive care physicians: a real-time observational study.
articles.abstract: Intensive care physicians make hundreds of decisions per shift under sustained cognitive and emotional demands. Decision fatigue, the tendency towards less effortful choices as cumulative decision load increases, may affect clinician wellbeing and decision processes. However, the associations of decision volume and temporal workload structure with within-shift fatigue and mood in intensive care unit (ICU) physicians remain unclear. This study explored whether decision volume and temporal clustering show distinct associations with fatigue, sleepiness, mood, and post-shift decision responses. Five physicians (two residents, three consultants) at a surgical ICU of a German university hospital were shadowed during 38 twelve-hour shifts (456 hours) between October and December 2025. Clinical decisions were classified by severity using a study-specific, non-validated Decision Severity Score. Because recruitment was feasibility-based and involved only five physicians, all analyses were considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Psychometric assessments of decision fatigue, sleepiness, and mood (Decision Fatigue Scale, Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, Profile of Mood States - Short Form) were administered at morning, midday, and shift end. Following each shift, physicians completed a standardised scenario task requiring three binary treatment decisions. Temporal workload structure was quantified using the burstiness metric; shifts were classified into four types by median split of decision density and burstiness (quiet-smooth, quiet-clustered, busy-smooth, busy-clustered). Linear and binomial mixed-effects models with physician as random intercept were used throughout. Across 17,953 recorded decisions (median 474 per shift; range 366-589), a higher mean decision rate was associated with greater end-of-shift decision fatigue: an increase of 0.5 decisions per 5-minute interval corresponded to a 2.1-point higher decision-fatigue score (95 % CI 0.6 to 3.6). Higher burstiness was associated with less mood disturbance, with a 0.10 increase in burstiness corresponding to a 6.3-point lower mood score (95% CI -10.2 to -2.3). Averaged across all shifts, changes between morning and evening were small and not statistically significant for any of the three scores. Within-shift trajectories differed by shift type, however, with mood disturbance increasing over the shift in quiet-smooth shifts only, a difference already apparent at midday. Quiet-smooth shifts, the least objectively demanding, showed the least favourable psychometric values. Response certainty in the post-shift scenario task was lower after shifts with more task interruptions, with each ten additional interruptions corresponding to a 0.29-point lower certainty score (p = 0.012), whilst a descriptive trend towards more conservative scenario responses was observed in busy-clustered shifts (odds ratio 2.25, p = 0.555). Decision volume and temporal workload structure showed different associations with psychometric outcomes: higher decision rates were associated with greater end-of-shift decision fatigue, whereas greater temporal clustering was associated with lower mood disturbance, already apparent from midday onwards. That more quiet, uniformly paced shifts showed the least favourable psychometric values suggests that reducing decision volume alone may not improve physician wellbeing; this observation requires replication. Mitigation strategies may therefore need to extend beyond reducing decision volume to protecting concentrated, meaningful clinical activity and minimising hindrance stressors such as interruptions. Future multicentre studies should determine whether these associations are reproducible and whether temporal workload structure is related to objective decision quality or patient-safety outcomes. German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00037564. Registered 27th August 2025.

Effect of clarithromycin on the circulating inflammatory proteome in community-acquired pneumonia: a secondary analysis of the ACCESS trial.
articles.abstract: The ACCESS randomized double-blind controlled trial in hospitalized adults with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) showed that adding clarithromycin to standard-of-care therapy accelerated clinical recovery within the first 72 hours after the commencement of treatment and reduced progression to organ dysfunction. Does clarithromycin treatment modulate the circulating inflammatory protein profile in CAP, and can inflammatory endotypes identify patient subgroups with distinct clinical responses? Serum samples obtained from ACCESS trial patients at baseline and 72 hours were profiled using the Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel. Patients were grouped by treatment arm and by achievement of the trial's composite primary endpoint. After quality control, 70 proteins from 394 paired samples across 197 patients were analyzed to assess differential expression within and between groups over time, evaluate associations with clinical outcomes, and identify immune endotypes using unsupervised clustering. IL6 was selectively downregulated on day 4 in the clarithromycin arm, whereas IFN-γ, CXCL9, CXCL10, and SCF decreased over time across both treatment arms, consistent with resolution of inflammation. Among patients achieving the primary endpoint, IL6, CXCL9, CXCL10, and IFN-γ were suppressed only in clarithromycin-treated individuals. Clustering consistently identified two inflammatory endotypes with comparable SOFA, but distinct RSS scores. The endotype with lower RSS demonstrated higher IFN-γ and globally elevated inflammatory protein expression; in that endotype 90-day mortality was decreased with clarithromycin treatment. Clarithromycin exerts measurable immunomodulatory effects in CAP, characterized by attenuation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL6. The identification of distinct inflammatory endotypes suggests biological heterogeneity in CAP and supports future investigation of endotype-guided approaches to identify patients most likely to benefit from immunomodulatory therapies. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04724044, EudraCT 2020-004452-15.

Trends in mortality rates in hypotensive pediatric trauma patients undergoing emergent trauma laparotomy.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Massive hemorrhage remains the leading cause of preventable death after pediatric trauma. Emergent trauma laparotomy (ETL) is a common operation to obtain hemorrhage control. Mortality rates for adult patients in hemorrhagic shock requiring ETL remain high and unchanged. Information on mortality rates after ETL in pediatric patients is limited. We sought to evaluate trends in mortality rates for pediatric ETL patients. The National Trauma Data Bank (NTDB) was queried from 2007 to 2023. Patients aged 0 to 18 years old were included if they underwent ETL. ETL was defined as laparotomy within 1 hour of arrival. Hypotension was defined as a systolic blood pressure <90 mm Hg on arrival. The primary outcome was annual hospital mortality rates for hypotensive patients requiring ETL. Secondary outcomes included annual 24-hour mortality rates for both hypotensive and all patients requiring ETL. Mortality rates were compared in 5-year cohorts to reduce annual variability. A total of 11,374 patients underwent ETL. The majority of patients were male (79%; n=78,963/11,374). Most patients were between the ages of 12 and 17 (84%; n=9,565/11,374), followed by ages 5 to 11 (11%; n=1,227/11,374), then ages 0 to 4 (5%; n=582/11,374). Penetrating injuries predominated (69%; n=7,866/11,374). The hospital mortality rate for all patients was 18.3% (n=2,079/11,374). Of patients who died, 74% were within 24 hours of arrival (n=1,533/2,079). Overall, 19% (n=2,125/11,374) were hypotensive on arrival. For hypotensive patients, the 24-hour and hospital mortality rates were 30% (n=641/2,125) and 45.9% (n=976/2,125). There was year-to-year variability in rates of hospital mortality of hypotensive patients through the study period (p<0.001). However, the average mortality rates from 2007 to 2011 (45%; n=293/645) and 2019 to 2023 (42%; n=266/638) were unchanged (p=0.95). Pediatric trauma patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage requiring ETL continue to suffer high rates of mortality. These findings underscore the urgent need for targeted research and performance improvement. Prognostic and Epidemiological; Level III.

articles.title: Opioid prescribing and hospital outcomes after trauma in patients with substance use disorder: An analysis of the michigan trauma quality improvement project.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Trauma patients frequently have comorbid substance use disorders (SUD), which may complicate pain management and increase the risk of opioid-related adverse outcomes after discharge. We hypothesized that trauma patients with SUD would be prescribed more opioids at discharge than those without SUD. We retrospectively analyzed a cohort of adult trauma patients across the state from 2022 to 2025 using a statewide collaborative database. Primary outcomes were opioid prescription at discharge (yes/no) and amount prescribed standardized to oxycodone 5 mg pills. A multivariable approach assessed risk-adjusted differences in outcomes among patients with SUD versus without SUD. Among 29,805 total patients, 8,672 (29.1%) had a diagnosis of SUD. 71.2% of patients with SUD received a discharge opioid prescription, compared with 59.6% of patients without SUD (p<0.001). After adjustment, the predicted probability of receiving an opioid prescription at discharge was 64.2% (95% CI, 63.1%-65.2%) for patients with SUD and 62.5% (95% CI, 62.0%-63.1%) for those without. Among patients that received a prescription, those with SUD were prescribed 21.2 pills of 5 mg oxycodone, corresponding to an adjusted difference of 1.6 additional pills (95% CI, 0.89-2.31; p<0.001) compared with those without. Prescribing patterns also differed by race and ethnicity: Hispanic or Latino patients were 5.4-percentage points more likely to receive an opioid prescription than non-Hispanic or Latino patients, while, among prescription recipients, Black patients received 3.56 fewer pills than White patients. Our findings demonstrate that patients with SUD received opioids more frequently and in greater amounts at discharge, yet absolute differences were small in magnitude and may not represent clinically meaningful differences. Differences in prescribing by race and ethnicity were larger in magnitude and warrant further investigation. Prognostic and epidemiological; Level III.

articles.title: In older adults, "mild" by GCS does not mean low risk: Multicenter study of 1,157 patients with mild TBI and acute subdural hematoma.
authors: Traumatic Subdural Hematoma Outcomes Study Group
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Acute traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) is the most common intracranial injury in mild TBI (mTBI), particularly in older adults. However, the relationship of patient and brain computed tomography (CT) characteristics with outcomes remains poorly described in a contemporary cohort. This study aims to characterize outcomes in younger and older adults with mTBI and isolated acute SDH. This was a 10-center, retrospective cohort study of adult traumas with emergency department Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 13 to 15 and acute traumatic SDH on initial brain CT ('22-'23). Trauma registry, EHR, and Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) data were collected through automated and manual methods. The primary outcome was total mortality (TM=death+hospice discharge); the sample was stratified by 18 to 64 versus older than or equal to 65 years. Multivariable backward selection logistic regression examined 21 demographic, injury, and brain CT covariates. In total, 1,157 patients were included (18-64 y: 28%; ≥65 y: 72%; 58% transferred in). Median [IQR] non-head ISS was 1 [1-5] in 18 to 64 years, and 1 [1-2] in older than or equal to 65 years. Ten percent had neurosurgical intervention (18-64 y: 8%; ≥65 y: 11%). TM was higher in older than or equal to 65 years than 18 to 64 years (10% vs. 3%). Compared with older than or equal to 65 years, 18 to 64 years were discharged home more frequently (78% vs. 51%) and to hospice less frequently (2% vs. 7%). In 18 to 64 years, factors associated with TM were race, advance directive, functional dependence, ISS, more midline shift, and thicker SDH (too few TMs for adjusted models). In older than or equal to 65 years, factors independently associated with TM were advance directive (aOR [95% CI]: 11.8 [2.9-49.0]), male sex (3.0 [1.3-7.0]), midline shift (1.8 [1.3-2.6]), shock index (1.5 [1.1-2.1]), and worsening SDH on follow-up CT (2.9 [1.3-6.6]). Despite presenting as "mild", these data highlight that older adults with SDH have high TM and should continue to receive the highest-level care with timely goals-of-care discussions. The association between advance directives and TM should be interpreted within the context of baseline vulnerability and preinjury treatment preferences, not as a biological mortality predictor. Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

articles.title: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Achieve Provincial Implementation of a Web-Based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) Survey to Inform Patient-Centered Care.
articles.abstract: To review the web-based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) survey across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs to capture patient and family experiences with critical care, and to evaluate feasibility, participation, and satisfaction scores. A province-wide, multisite quality improvement study using an electronic, key-based FS-ICU survey with prospectively collected anonymous data linked to encounters through a centralized database. All 83 adult level 3 ICUs (52 community, 31 academic) in ON, Canada, from July 1, 2019, to May 31, 2024. The population comprised adult ICU patients, family members, or substitute decision-makers, with one survey per ICU encounter regardless of length of stay or number of family members. ICUs implemented a web-based FS-ICU using a unique seven-digit key in three formats (Staff-Provided, Quick Response-Driven, Website-Code), supported by training, resources, and tablets, with no clinical care interventions beyond routine practice. Feasibility metrics included onboarding (keys generated per ICU admission), opening, participation, and completion rates, calculated for different centers using provincial data. Over the study period, 24,679 unique keys were generated for 353,400 ICU admissions (onboarding rate, 7.0%), 13,596 keys were opened (opening rate, 55.1%), and 7,542 surveys met the greater than or equal to 70% completion threshold (completion rate, 57.6% among opened surveys; reflection rate, 2.1% of ICU encounters). Survey initiation was highest with the Staff-Provided format (88.4% of keys initiated), and overall satisfaction was high, with mean FS with Care, 87.8; FS with Decision-Making, 84.4; and FS-TOTAL 86.5 on a 0-100 scale, with nursing care rated highest and adequacy of time for questions rated lowest. A provincial, web-based FS-ICU was implemented across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs, producing a large dataset with high satisfaction scores. A small proportion completed the survey, highlighting feasibility and workflow barriers. Future efforts should improve activation and completion rates and integrate FS-ICU data into routine quality improvement to enhance patient- and family-centered care.

articles.title: ICU Physical Environments Used for Family Conferences: A Multimodal Qualitative Evaluation with ICU Team Members.
articles.abstract: Family-clinician communication is central to high-quality care for critically ill patients. Although previous work has focused on improving how and what is communicated, little is known about where this high-stakes communication takes place and how it is shaped by the physical environment. Our objectives were to characterize ICU spaces typically used for family conferences and identify modifiable environmental features that influence communication. We conducted a multimodal qualitative study of 17 spaces typically used for family conferences across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. Healthcare design and architecture experts independently assessed architectural plans and photographs to characterize spatial features. Then, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 ICU team members (nurses, social workers, case managers) to elicit perspectives on and experiences within these spaces. We conducted qualitative content analysis using a combined inductive and deductive approach. A total of 17 family conference spaces across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. A total of 23 ICU team members. None. The 17 analyzed spaces included designated family-communication rooms (n = 2), multipurpose rooms (n = 6), visitor lounges (n = 4), and public areas (n = 5; lobbies/hallways). Study participants preferred designated spaces, as they provide privacy, prevent interruption, and facilitate emotional support. Conversely, multipurpose and public areas are prone to distractions and interruptions from conflicting uses. We identified key environmental features that support communication: proximity to patients, flexible furniture layout, and nonclinical ambiance. Family conferences occur in a variety of physical environments in and around adult ICUs, ranging from intentionally designed rooms to elevator lobbies. ICU team members perceive that physical environments have an important influence on communication quality, and we identified pragmatic opportunities to improve existing spaces.

articles.title: Multicompartmental hemorrhage: A high-risk pattern associated with increased risk for progression in TBI patients.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) often requires repeat head computed tomography (CT) imaging to monitor for bleed progression. While prior literature has explored patient-level factors, data on the impact of ICH morphologies (subdural [SDH], epidural [EDH], intraparenchymal [IPH], intraventricular [IVH], and multicompartment hemorrhage [MCH]) on radiographic ICH progression remains unclear. We hypothesized that MCH and IVH would have an increased associated risk of progression. This retrospective (2021-2023) single-center cohort included adults (≥18 y) with TBI-related ICH who underwent initial and repeat head CT. Patients were stratified into radiographic progression versus no-progression cohorts, with progression defined as new or enlarging hemorrhage on attending radiologist interpretation of follow-up head CT. The primary outcome was the rate of radiographic progression for each ICH type. MCH was defined as the presence of two or more ICH types. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to evaluate the association between each ICH type and radiographic progression, adjusting for age, mechanism of injury, Injury Severity Score, Glasgow Coma Scale on arrival, trauma-bay intubation, and preinjury antithrombotic exposure. Of the 817 patients with ICH on initial head CT and documented repeat CT, 401 (49.1%) had radiographic progression. Patients with progression were younger (58 vs. 62 y, p=0.027), more frequently male (71.3% vs. 63.7%, p=0.020), and had similar antithrombotic exposure (15.2% vs. 14.2%, p=0.678). Craniotomy/craniectomy was more frequent among those with progression (21.2% vs. 8.2%, p<0.001). On multivariable analysis, MCH demonstrated the strongest associated risk for progression (odds ratio [OR] 5.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.36-9.33, p<0.001), whereas IPH (OR 2.02, CI: 0.86-4.75, p=0.108), SDH, EDH, and IVH were not independently associated with radiographic ICH progression. MCH was independently associated with radiographic ICH progression. This higher-risk hemorrhage pattern may warrant closer neurological monitoring. Prognostic/Epidemiologic; Level III.

articles.title: A clinically relevant porcine model of flail chest: Development and multimodal validation.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Flail chest has high mortality, but large-animal models with thoracic anatomy comparable to humans are lacking. The objective of this study was to develop a clinically relevant porcine flail chest model that preserves pleural, pulmonary, and neurovascular integrity, and to validate it using multimodal assessment including computed tomography (CT) imaging and physiologic parameters. Twelve male Landrace pigs were randomly assigned to a flail chest (FC) group and a multiple single rib fracture (MRF) group (n=6 per group). Under general anesthesia, controlled osteotomies were performed on the fifth to eighth ribs. The intercostal neurovascular bundle was protected, and the parietal pleura was bluntly separated before each osteotomy to preserve pleural integrity. In the FC group, each rib was transected at two sites to create a four-rib flail segment; in the MRF group, a single transection was made per rib. Paradoxical chest wall motion was visually confirmed in the FC group before layered closure. Invasive arterial pressure, heart rate, pulse oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and end‑tidal carbon dioxide tension (ETCO₂) were monitored throughout. Chest CT was performed on Day 7. All surgeries were successful, with no mortality. Paradoxical chest wall motion was confirmed in all FC animals after emergence. The SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio declined postoperatively in both groups, with a significantly greater decrease in the FC group than in the MRF group (221.0±1.4 vs. 260.2±1.9, P<0.001). Heart rate and mean arterial pressure increased in both groups and were significantly higher in the FC group (P<0.001). CT confirmed the intended fracture patterns and flail-segment displacement, with no evidence of pleural breach, pulmonary injury, pneumothorax, or hemothorax. A standardized porcine flail chest model was established that preserves pleural, pulmonary, and neurovascular integrity, allowing the isolated study of rib fracture pathophysiology. This model will facilitate future research on fixation materials and surgical techniques. Basic Science/ Animal Study.

articles.title: Contemporary management of traumatic abdominal wall hernias: What you need to know.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Traumatic abdominal wall hernia (TAWH) is an uncommon but clinically important consequence of both blunt and penetrating abdominal trauma. It is defined by disruption of the abdominal wall musculature and fascia with herniation of intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal contents through the defect. Although penetrating abdominal wall defects are usually apparent and can often be primarily closed during operative exploration, blunt TAWH is significantly more heterogeneous and challenging. The skin may remain intact while the muscle, fascia, neurovascular supply, and bony attachments are disrupted. The reported incidence of TAWH varies according to imaging strategy and trauma population, but frank herniation remains rare, occurring in <1% of blunt trauma patients in most contemporary series. The major management challenge is deciding whether the patient requires immediate trauma laparotomy or laparoscopy, acute abdominal wall repair, staged management with same-admission repair, or delayed hernia repair/abdominal wall reconstruction. Evidence remains primarily dominated by retrospective single-center series, multicenter registry studies, and systematic reviews with heterogeneous definitions and follow-up. Although traditional dogma had taught that these repairs should always be performed in a delayed fashion, recent multicenter data, systematic reviews, and surgeon experience suggest that timing of repair, type of repair, and mesh use must be individualized; bowel injury, contamination, defect location, and patient physiology are more important than a universal early-versus-delayed algorithm. This article summarizes the practical issues the trauma and acute care surgeon needs to know: diagnosis, classification, associated injuries, indications for exploration, repair timing, operative strategy, management of lateral and posterior defects, mesh use in contaminated fields, and associated outcomes.

Weaning Strategies for High-Flow Nasal Cannula in Critically Ill Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: This study evaluated the efficacy of different high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) weaning protocols in critically ill adults. This multicenter, randomized controlled trial was conducted from December 1, 2022, to August 31, 2024, based on the suggested protocol (SLOWH trial). Experts reviewed the trial between October 2, 2024, and April 15, 2025. Randomization was performed by a research coordinator using a sequence of random numbers generated by an independent statistician blinded to both researchers and participants. Adults (≥ 18 yr old) in the ICU who met the weaning criteria after receiving HFNC were included. Among 102 patients from three tertiary care hospitals, 15 were excluded. The remaining patients were randomized into three intervention groups: flow reduction (FR) first, Fio2 reduction (OR) first, or simultaneous reduction (SR). The primary outcome was the HFNC weaning success rate, defined as successful transition to conventional oxygen therapy without the need for HFNC reapplication, noninvasive ventilation, or endotracheal intubation within 24 hours. A total of 87 adults completed the trial (FR, n = 31 [male, 52%]; OR, n = 26 [male, 77%]; SR, n = 30 [male, 53%]). The weaning success rates in the FR, OR, and SR groups were 94%, 81%, and 77%, respectively (p = 0.15). The median [interquartile range] weaning duration was 31.0 hours (29.0-45.8 hr), 29.5 hours (28.0-60.4 hr), and 29.5 hours (26.5-45.0 hr) in the FR, OR, and SR groups, respectively, with no statistically significant difference among groups (p = 0.87). In this randomized trial, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three HFNC weaning strategies in terms of weaning success or duration.

articles.title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
authors: and the Padova Intensive Care Unit (PADUA-ICU) Group
articles.abstract: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality. Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty). The intervention did not affect the ICU length of stay (MD, 4.21 d; 95% CI, -4.65 to 13.07 d; very low certainty), the rates of hospital-acquired infections (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.81-1.23; low certainty), or ICU mortality (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.72-1.08; very low certainty). Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.

articles.title: Developing Models for Complicated Outcomes in Acutely Intoxicated ICU Patients With and Without Toxicity Information.
authors: and the INTOXICATE Study Investigators Group
articles.abstract: To assess the prognostic value of the mean Lethality Risk Score (LRS), reflecting the toxicity of substances involved in an exposure, and to develop prediction models for complicated outcomes in ICU patients with acute intoxication. Multicenter prospective cohort study. Seventy-eight ICUs in Europe, Australia, and the Eastern Mediterranean (2020-2023). A total of 2265 adult patients were admitted to the ICU with acute intoxication as the main reason for admission for at least 4 hours. None. The primary outcome was defined as ICU complications or death (22.5%). Clinical data were collected in an electronic capture system. We developed two prediction models: one incorporating laboratory variables ("Laboratory Model"), and one including the mean LRS ("Expo Model"). The mean LRS was calculated as the average of the individual LRS values assigned to the toxicants involved in the exposure. Key predictors were age, severity at presentation, systolic blood pressure, Glasgow Coma Scale score, and hospital type. The mean LRS remained significant only when laboratory variables were not considered. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC), calibration plots, likelihood ratio tests, and decision curve analysis. Internal validation demonstrated good performance for both models (AUROCs of 0.79 and 0.77; calibration slopes of 0.94 and 0.95; intercepts of -0.06 and -0.06), with minimal overfitting. Decision curve analysis revealed clinically relevant threshold probability ranges of 0-50% for the Laboratory Model and 0-40% for the Expo Model. The mean LRS had prognostic value only in the absence of laboratory test results. Both models may aid decision-making regarding the management of acutely intoxicated patients in the ICU.

articles.title: Association of Tele-Critical Care Capability With Interhospital Transfers and Potentially Low-Value Transfers Among Critically Ill Medicare Beneficiaries.
articles.abstract: Interhospital transfer is essential for accessing specialized critical care services, yet it poses clinical risk and substantial burden for patients and the healthcare system. Tele-critical care (TCC) programs extend expertise to resource-limited hospitals and may influence transfer decisions by identifying patients requiring escalation or supporting local management. We examined the association between TCC capability at index ICU hospitalizations, interhospital transfer, and post-transfer outcomes. Nationwide retrospective cohort study using 2021-2023 Medicare claims linked to the American Hospital Association Annual Survey Database (AHAASD). U.S. acute care hospitals. Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries with ICU hospitalizations between 2022 and 2023. None. TCC capability was identified by AHAASD reporting and/or the presence of five or more TCC claims annually. The primary outcome was interhospital ICU transfer. Exploratory post-transfer outcomes included receipt of specialty procedures, death or hospice discharge within 1 day of transfer, in-hospital and 30-day mortality, and discharge disposition. Hierarchical logistic regression adjusted for patient demographics, comorbidities, acute organ failures, and transferring/accepting hospital characteristics, with transferring hospitals as random intercepts. Among 2,140,919 ICU hospitalizations, 33.4% occurred at 1,066 TCC-capable hospitals. Absolute transfer rates were similar (2.5% vs. 3.0%), but TCC capability was associated with higher adjusted odds of transfer (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% CI, 1.01-1.14). In exploratory post-transfer analyses, transferred patients from TCC hospitals had greater illness severity yet were less likely to die or be discharged to hospice within 1 day of transfer (4.6% vs. 6.6%; aOR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.76-0.97) and more likely to be discharged home within 2 days (4.7% vs. 3.7%; aOR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.03-1.33). TCC capability was associated with modestly increased transfer rates, fewer potentially low-value transfers, and improved post-transfer outcomes, suggesting improved transfer selection.

articles.title: Ventilatory Management in Neurocritical Versus Non-Neurocritical Care Patients: A Pooled Analysis From the PRIME Database.
authors: PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS (PRoVENT), PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries (PRoVENT-iMiC), and Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes (ENIO) investigators
articles.abstract: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality. Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database. PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS" (PRoVENT), "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries" (PRoVENT-iMiC), and "Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes" (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation. Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao2/Fio2 ratio. This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (Vts), positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median Vt and higher Fio2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. Vt normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS. In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like Vt, positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

articles.title: Pediatric Clinical Interventions and Adverse Safety Events Among Emergency Medical Services Encounters in Agencies With and Without a Pediatric Emergency Care Coordinator: An Observational Study.
articles.abstract: The purpose of this study was to compare the frequency and types of adverse safety events (ASEs) and potential harm in a diverse population of pediatric emergency medical services (EMS) encounters. As a secondary aim we evaluated the association between prehospital pediatric emergency care coordinators (PECCs) in EMS agencies on the frequency, type and harm severity of ASEs. This was a cross-sectional study of EMS and hospital records for children <18 years who received care from 15 EMS agencies from 2019 to 2023, using a validated ASE chart review tool. Frequency and types of ASEs associated with three different categories of clinical interventions (procedures, medication, and fluid administration) were captured. ASEs were assigned to three severities of harm: Harm Unlikely, Mild Temporary Harm, or Permanent/Severe Harm. EMS Physicians verified ASEs and harm severity. There were 2219 records included in the analysis, 995 from PECC agencies (44.8%). Median patient age was 12.5 years (IQR 6-15). In total, 551 (55.4%; CI: 52.3, 58.5) PECC agency patients had a procedure compared to 328 patients of agencies without a PECC (26.8%; CI: 24.3, 29.3; p < 0.001). Compared to non-PECC agency patients, PECC agency patients were more likely to receive medications (23.4% vs 7.7%, p< 0.001) and receive intravenous fluids (12.9% vs 4.6%, p< 0.001). In total, 290 ASEs were identified, the most frequent of which was the failure to perform a procedure or administer a medication or fluids (43.1%, CI: 37.4, 48.8). There were differences between PECC and non-PECC agencies in the frequency of ASEs in procedures (13.7% vs, 20.0%, p = 0.003). The assigned severity of ASE Mild Temporary and Permanent/Severe Harm was lower for procedures in PECC versus non-PECC agencies, respectively (28.6%, CI: 29.5, 48.5 and 63.3%, 95% CI: 69.6, 88.4, p < 0.001). Compared to non-PECC agency care, pediatric care by PECC agencies was associated with more procedures, medication and fluid administration, but fewer ASEs for procedures and lower severity of harm when an ASE occurred. These results indicate that the PECC role may be associated with increased interventions and a reduction in harm associated with procedural care.
